stage_state.summary_md:
## Retirement Announcement and Aftermath

BA and Air France couldn't coordinate—Air France retired in May while BA planned October. A Forum 150 meeting shifted from April 9th (the 34th anniversary of first flight) to April 10th.

Bannister presented in uniform to senior management, hitting the "Marmite factor": roughly two-thirds expressed sadness, the remainder relief. He introduced the line that became universally adopted: "It's the right decision at the right time for the right reasons."

When Branson offered to take Concorde, BA said government funding meant the transfer decision wasn't theirs. A senior Virgin pilot later told Bannister "not a chance in hell"—Concorde "would probably send us bust."

Another common question: retain one aircraft for air shows? Impossible—Concorde required a Certificate of Airworthiness and Type Certificate, far higher standards than a "Permit to Fly." Infrastructure costs of £60 million per annum would rise by another £40 million and couldn't shrink with fleet reduction. Airbus refused to transfer the Type Certificate because air-intake technology remained proprietary and used on military aircraft.

As discussion shifted from motives to legacy, Edward de Bono observed that Concorde appealed to both brain hemispheres—technologically superb and artistically graceful. Most Brits felt individual ownership: "That's my Concorde up there."
